title: Taking pieces: is the capture safe?
outcomes: Finds a capture that wins an undefended piece
Checks whether the target is defended before taking
Knows that a capture is never forced and that a king cannot be captured
Chooses the cheapest piece to capture with, and spots defenders that are far away or that do not really defend
Explains in their own words why to check who can take back before capturing

steps.text: Look at the next board before you read on. A lone black pawn stands on e5 with no black piece beside it, and the white queen can take it. Would you? Decide first, then watch. [H] Our guess is that many new players say yes, because nothing is next to the pawn.

steps.caption: Nothing stands next to the pawn. The bishop on b8 is far away, but it looks along a long diagonal.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn. It looks like a free pawn.
The bishop slides down the long diagonal and takes the queen. A pawn cost White a queen.

claims.statement: The bishop on b8 defends the pawn on e5.
Qxe5 Bxe5 gives a queen for a pawn.

steps.text: A **capture** is a move onto a square where an enemy piece stands. You remove that piece and your own piece takes its place. Almost every piece captures exactly the way it normally moves, so there is nothing new to learn for them. Pawns have two twists, shown next. You can only take enemy pieces, never your own.

steps.caption: The bishop moves along its diagonal and lands on the knight. The knight leaves the board for good.

line.say: The bishop slides up its diagonal to e5, lands on the knight and removes it.
Black has no piece that can take the bishop, so Black simply makes another move.

claims.statement: Bxe5 wins the knight and White keeps the bishop.
No black piece defends the knight.

steps.caption: The queen captures the way it moves, along a file, a rank or a diagonal. Here it uses the b-file.

line.say: The queen slides up the file past two empty squares, lands on the bishop and removes it.
Nothing can take the queen on b4, so Black moves on.

claims.statement: Nothing defends the bishop on b4.
Qxb4 wins the bishop for nothing.

steps.caption: The knight jumps in its L shape and captures only where it lands. Pieces in between do not matter.

line.say: The knight jumps to e5, lands on the rook and removes it.
Black can attack the knight with a pawn, but the rook is already gone.

claims.statement: Nxe5 is legal.
Nothing defends the rook on e5.
Nxe5 wins the rook, which is worth more than the knight.

steps.caption: A pawn moves straight ahead but captures one step diagonally forward. The black pawn in front is just in the way.

line.say: The pawn captures diagonally forward onto d5 and takes the knight.
Nothing of Black's can take the pawn back.

claims.statement: The pawn cannot capture straight ahead on e5.
The pawn can capture diagonally on d5.
Nothing defends the knight on d5.
exd5 leaves White at least 2 points ahead along the engine line.

steps.caption: Pawn twist one: en passant. Black's pawn has just jumped two squares past the white pawn. For this one move only, White may take it as if it had stopped a square short.

line.say: The pawn captures diagonally onto d6, the square the black pawn jumped over, and the pawn on d5 is removed.
Black moves on. The chance to capture this way was only for that one move.

claims.statement: exd6 en passant is legal.
The pawn cannot simply move straight onto d5.

steps.caption: Pawn twist two: a pawn that captures onto the last row must also promote, which means it changes into another piece. Here it takes a knight and becomes a queen.

line.say: The pawn captures diagonally onto b8 and promotes to a queen at the same moment.
Black has no piece left to take the new queen.

claims.statement: axb8=Q is legal.
Capturing and promoting wins the knight and more.

steps.text: Before you take, ask one question: **can the enemy take back?** A piece is **defended** when a friend could capture on its square if you took it; that capture back is a **recapture**. A piece that is attacked and not defended is **loose**. Taking a loose piece usually wins it, but a loose piece can still be bait, as you will see.

steps.caption: The same kind of capture, one difference: a pawn stands behind the target. Watch what Black can do.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn on e5.
The pawn on d6 captures diagonally onto e5 and takes the bishop back.

claims.statement: The pawn on d6 defends e5.
Bxe5 dxe5 gives a bishop for a pawn.

steps.caption: Two loose pieces can be taken. When you can only take one, usually take the more valuable (a rule of thumb).

line.say: The knight takes the rook, the bigger prize.
Black's bishop escapes, but White has won a whole rook.

claims.statement: Nothing defends the rook on b5.
Nothing defends the bishop on e6.
Nxb5 wins the rook.

steps.title: Same capture, one change
steps.prompt: The queen on d4 could take the knight on b6. Predict first, then check. In the second position a pawn defends the knight; in the third a pawn stands nearby but defends nothing.

steps.text: Not every defended piece is safe from you. Compare what each side gives up. As a **rule of thumb** (a guide, not a law) we count a pawn as 1 point, a knight or bishop as 3, a rook as 5 and a queen as 9. If you win more points than you lose back, the capture can pay even when the piece is defended.

steps.caption: A queen takes a pawn: a poor trade in points when a pawn can take back.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn on d5.
The pawn on c6 takes the queen. White gave 9 points for 1.

claims.statement: The pawn on c6 defends d5.
Qxd5 cxd5 loses the queen for a pawn.

steps.caption: The rook is defended, but the knight is worth less than a rook. Watch the count.

line.say: The knight takes the rook on e6, a 5-point piece.
The pawn takes the knight back. White gave 3 points and won 5.

claims.statement: The pawn on f7 defends e6.
Nxe6 fxe6 wins 2 points.

steps.caption: A pawn takes a knight that a queen defends. The pawn is the cheapest piece White can lose.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight on c5.
The queen takes the pawn back. White gave 1 point and won 3.

claims.statement: The queen on d6 defends c5.
bxc5 Qxc5 wins 2 points.

steps.caption: Sometimes the swap is exactly even: a knight for a knight. Neither side gains.

line.say: The knight takes the knight on c6.
The pawn takes the knight back. Each side lost 3 points.

claims.statement: The pawn on b7 defends c6.
Nxc6 bxc6 is an even swap.

steps.text: Why only a guide? The numbers are averages for ordinary positions. [S] In my summary of Edward Lasker's strategy book, a piece is worth what it can do, so a rook with no file to use may be worth less than five (sources/sheets, K5). [I] A knight stuck on the edge is probably worth less than three. [H] Trust the numbers first, doubt them second.

**Count the squad.** Often several pieces can capture on one square. Count the attackers and the defenders. Here White has two attackers on the knight and Black has one defender. Order matters: take first with the cheaper piece, so the second attacker is still waiting when the defender takes back.

steps.caption: Two white attackers against one black defender, capture by capture.

line.say: White's first attacker, the knight, takes the knight.
Black's only defender takes back, and the pawn leaves d6.
White's second attacker, the rook, takes the pawn. Black has no defender left.
Black moves on. White won a knight and a pawn and lost a knight.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack e5.
One black piece defends e5.
The sequence wins a pawn.

steps.text: Two questions cover most cases. Can anything take back? If nothing can, the capture wins the piece for now; still look at what else the move changes (a trapped capturer, a piece you uncover, a check on your king). If something can, count the points: what you take against what you could lose. A swap of equal pieces is an **even trade**; whether to make one depends on the position.

steps.caption: A preview: a free-looking capture that still loses. The pawn on a7 is loose, but taking it traps the bishop.

line.say: The bishop takes the loose pawn.
Black attacks the bishop with a pawn. Every square the bishop can reach is covered.
White cannot save it.
The king walks over and takes the bishop next.

claims.statement: Nothing defends the pawn on a7.
Bxa7 is clearly worse than the best move.

steps.caption: A black piece stands right beside the knight, but it only matters if it can capture on d5.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight on d5.
The black bishop moves along a diagonal of the other colour and cannot take back on d5.

claims.statement: No black piece defends d5.
Bxd5 wins at least 3 points.

steps.caption: The defender can be far away. A rook on the same open file guards the bishop from the other end of the board.

line.say: The queen takes the bishop on d5.
The rook slides down the open d-file and takes the queen.

claims.statement: The rook on d8 defends d5 along the open file.
Qxd5 Rxd5 loses at least 6 points.

steps.caption: Two white pieces can take the same knight, which a pawn defends. Compare what each could lose.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight; the recapture costs only a pawn.
Black takes the pawn back. White gave 1 point and won 3.

claims.statement: The pawn on d6 defends e5.
fxe5 dxe5 wins 2 points.

steps.caption: The same position, but White takes with the queen. Now the recapture costs far more.

line.say: The queen takes the knight on e5.
The pawn takes the queen. White gave 9 points and won 3.

claims.statement: Qxe5 dxe5 loses at least 4 points.

steps.text: Taking with the cheapest piece is a **rule of thumb**, not a law. It fails when the cheap piece cannot take. A piece **pinned** to its king may not move off the line, because that would expose the king. A pinned piece cannot capture off that line, and it cannot recapture either: it defends only on paper.

steps.caption: The knight on c6 seems to defend e5, but the white bishop pins it to the king.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn.
Black cannot retake with the pinned knight, since the king would be in check. The king steps aside.

claims.statement: On paper the knight on c6 defends e5.
The pinned knight cannot capture on e5.
Nxe5 wins the pawn.

steps.caption: Scan before you take. The bishop on c6 is loose, and two white pieces attack it: the knight and the rook on c1. Take with the knight, the cheaper piece.

line.say: The knight takes the loose bishop. Nothing can take it back.
Black moves on.

claims.statement: Only the bishop on c6 is loose.
Nxc6 wins the bishop.

steps.caption: The same position, the other capture. The pawn on e6 is defended by the pawn on f7.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn.
The pawn takes back. White gave a knight (3 points) for a pawn (1).

claims.statement: The pawn on f7 defends e6.

steps.prompt: Look at the first board again without the arrows. Name every black piece that is attacked, then say which of them nothing defends. What did you find?

steps.caption: A capture can also answer a threat. The bishop attacks the rook, and a pawn can simply remove the bishop.

line.say: The pawn takes the attacker on c3, and the rook is safe again.
Black cannot take the pawn back. White has won the bishop and the rook is safe.

claims.statement: The bishop on c3 attacks the rook on e1.
Nothing defends the bishop.
bxc3 wins the bishop for nothing.

steps.text: A view from outside this course: the teacher Dan Heisman recommends listing every check, capture and threat your opponent has before you move [S, chess.com article]. [H] Our guess is that for a new player the most useful single habit is the capture question: what can the enemy take back?

steps.caption: You never have to capture. Here White declines and keeps the bishop.

line.say: White ignores the pawn and brings the king toward the middle.
Nothing was forced; both sides simply continue.

claims.statement: Capturing on e5 was possible.
Bxe5 is clearly worse than the best move.

steps.text: **Two more rules.** A capture is never forced: you may leave a piece alone. And a king is never captured. If a king is attacked, its player must deal with it at once, and the game ends by checkmate (a later lesson). A king can capture, but only a piece that nothing defends.

steps.caption: The king stands beside two black men. One is loose, the other is defended.

line.say: The king takes the loose pawn on d3; nothing defends it.
Black replies with a pawn move.

claims.statement: Kxd3 is legal.
Nothing defends the pawn on d3.
Kxe5 is illegal.
The pawn on d6 defends e5.

steps.prompt: Teach it. Explain to a friend who has never played why you ask who can take back before you capture, using the pawn on e5 from the first board as your example.

fields.label: Your explanation in your own words

steps.text: Check yourself against three points. First: the queen could reach the pawn, but a far-off bishop guarded it. Second: you count who can take back, near or far. Third: if somebody can, you compare the points won and lost, and you may always decline.

steps.prompt: How many of the three points did your explanation cover: none, one, two or all three? Which one would you add next time?
